pairs.grabber: A SILENT HOOK FAILURE CAN SKIP YOUR CHECKS.
THIS GRABBER IS FAR TOO LONG TO BE AN UPPERCASE HOOK LINE

write.body:
Hooks let you run your own commands before or after Claude Code uses a tool. Teams use them to block risky edits, run formatters and enforce rules on every change.

The trouble starts when a hook command fails in a way nobody sees. The agent keeps working, the check never ran, and the team assumes the rule still holds.

This happens because a hook is just a process. If it crashes, times out or exits with the wrong code, the result depends on how the hook reports the failure.

A safer setup takes three steps:
1. Make every hook exit with a clear code for pass and fail.
2. Log each run to a file you can read later.
3. Test the failure path on purpose before you rely on it.

Trade-offs to keep in mind:
- Strict hooks stop more mistakes but can block real work when they break.
- Logging adds a little noise, so keep the lines short and dated.

Treat a hook like production code. If you never watched it fail, you do not know what it does when it fails.
